help.intro: Numbers are the words you will say most often in a German-speaking country — prices at the till, platform numbers at the station, room numbers, your own age and phone number — and they are also the words most often misheard, because the German sounds are not the English ones. This exercise is pure sound: listen and repeat, from null to a price. Three sounds carry it: z is ts (zwei = 'tsvai', zwanzig = 'TSVAN-tsikh'), ei is 'eye' (drei, zwei), and the -ig at the end of the tens is a soft 'ikh', not 'ig'. Say each one three times, and say the price out loud the German way — euros, then cents.
help.tips[0].title: z = ts, ei = eye, -ig = ikh
help.tips[0].text: zwei 'tsvai', zehn 'tsayn', zwanzig 'TSVAN-tsikh', dreißig 'DRY-ssikh'. The ts is the sound at the end of English 'cats'.
help.tips[0].check.why: z is always ts, and -ig at the end is a soft “ikh”: FEER-tsikh.
help.tips[1].title: Prices: euros, then cents
help.tips[1].text: 3,50 € is 'drei Euro fünfzig'. No word for the comma, and Euro never takes an s.
help.tips[1].check.q: Which is the natural way to say 4,80 €?
help.tips[1].check.why: Euros first, then cents, with no word for the comma — and Euro never takes an s.
help.tips[2].title: Stress the first part
help.tips[2].text: SIEBzehn, VIERzig, EINundzwanzig. In compound numbers the very first syllable carries the weight; the rest is quick.
help.tips[2].check.q: Where does the stress go in neunzehn?
help.tips[2].check.why: In numbers the first part carries the weight and the rest is quick: NEUNzehn, like SIEBzehn.
help.remember[0]: Say your own phone number and age in German every day until they are automatic.
help.remember[1]: cats → zwei: the ts at the end of cats is the z at the start of every German number.
help.exam: A1 Sprechen: after your introduction the examiner asks you to spell a word and say a number — usually your phone number or postcode.
help.hook: Prices, platforms, phone numbers — numbers are what you'll say most, and three sounds make them sound truly German.
